Level 3: Component architecture

Chipset

A helper chip that adds extra connections: USB, SATA and more PCIe lanes.

What is it?

The chipset is a support chip, usually under a flat heatsink. In older PCs it did much more; today the CPU handles memory and graphics directly, and the chipset mainly adds extra I/O.

What does it do?

It connects USB ports, SATA drives, extra M.2 slots, network and audio chips, and passes their data to the CPU over one high-speed link.

Why it matters

The chipset model decides features like overclocking support and how many extra drives and USB ports a board has.

Real-life examples

  • AMD X870 / B650For AM5 Ryzen
  • Intel Z890For Core Ultra 200S
  • Intel Z790 / B760For 12th–14th gen Core

Key specifications

Link to CPU
PCIe 4.0 x4 or Intel DMI
Adds
USB, SATA, PCIe lanes
Cooling
usually a passive heatsink

How it connects

  • CPULinked by one fast connection
  • I/O portsDrives many of the USB ports
  • StorageAdds SATA and extra M.2 slots

Fun fact

Older PCs had two chipset chips: a “northbridge” for memory and graphics and a “southbridge” for slower I/O. The northbridge’s jobs have since moved into the CPU.
